fields.description_1:
Bluecenter offers several beauty treatments, but people do not compare facial care, permanent makeup, massage and laser hair removal in the same way. A visitor may start with a concern, a price question or a treatment name, and each route needs different practical information before an appointment makes sense.

The website therefore had to separate treatment categories without making the experience feel clinical or overwhelming. Prices and frequently asked questions needed to support decisions rather than sit far away from the service they explain. The portfolio story also has to avoid promising cosmetic or skin results that depend on the person and treatment. The challenge was to make treatment discovery, practical information and booking feel clear, calm and easy to use on mobile.
fields.description_2:
I organised Bluecenter around recognizable treatment categories, then placed prices, practical details and common questions close to the service where they matter. Visitors can understand the difference between facial treatments, permanent makeup, massage and laser hair removal before deciding whether to book or ask for more information.

Appointment actions remain visible after useful context instead of appearing as the only purpose of every section. I kept the language simple and avoided claims about guaranteed appearance or treatment outcomes. On smaller screens, treatment cards, price information and booking actions keep a clear reading order. The portfolio case now explains how the WordPress structure supports treatment comparison and appointment decisions without turning a beauty service into generic promotional copy.

fields.description_1:
Mdvinstallaties serves customers with very different technical needs. Someone planning electrical work or a renovation can take time to compare services, while a person needing maintenance or locksmith help may want a faster route to contact. Mixing those situations into one general services page would make both journeys harder.

The website needed to distinguish planned installation work from service and urgent support while still showing that they belong to the same company. Practical information had to appear before a visitor reaches contact, especially on mobile where long service lists become difficult to scan. The portfolio text also needed to avoid unsupported claims about response times or guaranteed repairs. The challenge was to make the type and urgency of the job clear from the first choices.
fields.description_2:
I structured Mdvinstallaties so planned installation work, renovations, maintenance and locksmith support each have a clear route. Customers can start from the job they need rather than reading a long company introduction, then see the practical information that helps them decide whether to request service or make direct contact.

Urgent-looking actions are kept separate from normal quotation or project enquiries, so the interface does not suggest that every request follows the same timetable. Headings stay practical, and the mobile layout keeps service choices and contact options easy to reach. The portfolio case now describes the real difference between project work and service support inside one WordPress site, without inventing response times, repair outcomes or other operational promises that were not independently verified.

fields.description_1:
Ckbouw needs to speak to two audiences that visit for different reasons. Project clients want to understand construction services and see relevant work, while job seekers need employer information, vacancies and a clear application route. If those journeys share the same priority everywhere, both can become harder to follow.

The website therefore needed an information structure that keeps commercial project content and recruitment content connected to one company without mixing their next steps. Project examples had to support the construction offer, while vacancies needed enough context to stand alone. Mobile navigation also had to make the audience choice obvious. The portfolio problem was to organise a construction company with client and candidate journeys, without inventing project results, hiring outcomes or generic claims about company culture.
fields.description_2:
I separated Ckbouw into a client route and a candidate route while keeping shared company information consistent. Construction services and completed projects help potential clients understand the type of work before making contact. Employer content and vacancies give job seekers a path to roles and application information without forcing them through commercial pages.

The two journeys meet only where shared context is useful, such as the company story or project environment. Calls to action are written for the audience using them instead of relying on one generic button. On mobile, service cards, project examples, vacancy links and application actions keep a predictable order. The portfolio case now shows how one WordPress website supports business development and recruitment without treating them as the same user task.

fields.description_1:
Prolineafbouw offers several finishing services that may appear similar to a visitor who is not familiar with construction terminology. Latex spraying, system ceilings, walls, metal-stud work, plastering and painting solve different parts of a project, so a simple list would not give property owners enough help to choose a route.

The website needed to explain those services separately, connect them with project examples and keep quotation actions close to the information that supports a decision. The case study also had to avoid promises about finish quality, speed or project results unless independently proven. On mobile, technical service names needed enough context to remain understandable. The challenge was to turn a broad finishing offer into clear choices without oversimplifying the work or repeating generic contractor wording.
fields.description_2:
I organised Prolineafbouw around individual finishing services so visitors can understand where latex spraying, ceilings, walls, metal-stud work, plastering and painting fit within a project. Each service can carry its own explanation and relevant examples before the visitor reaches a quotation or contact action.

Project imagery supports the service story instead of replacing it, and supporting details stay close to the work they describe. I kept headings direct and avoided vague phrases about perfect results or unmatched craftsmanship. On smaller screens, service choices, examples and quotation actions follow the same priority as desktop. The portfolio case now presents Prolineafbouw as a specialist finishing company with distinct work types and a practical enquiry path, rather than as another generic construction website.

fields.description_1:
Connectwerk has to serve candidates and employers from the same recruitment platform, but their goals are different. Candidates want vacancies, role details and an easy way to register or apply. Employers need to understand staffing support, sector knowledge and how to start a hiring conversation.

If both audiences receive the same page order and calls to action, vacancy content can overwhelm employer information or commercial messages can interrupt job search. The website needed a clear audience split while preserving sector context where useful. Mobile users need that distinction before opening lists or forms. The portfolio story had to describe the recruitment structure without claiming more placements, faster hiring or stronger application results. The challenge was to keep two journeys separate while maintaining one company experience.
fields.description_2:
I structured Connectwerk around two direct entry routes: finding work and finding staff. Candidates can move from vacancy discovery to role information, registration or application without passing through employer sales content. Employers can review staffing services and sector context before starting a conversation about their recruitment need.

Shared information is used only where both audiences benefit from it, so the site does not duplicate every section or mix unrelated calls to action. Vacancy cards, forms and employer contact actions keep their own priorities on mobile. I used plain labels that describe the next step instead of internal recruitment terminology. The portfolio case now explains how WordPress supports two connected but different recruitment journeys without making unverified claims about placement numbers, hiring speed or business performance.
